source.title: A common approach to three open problems in number theory

accepted.question_text: Let A be the set of all equations of the forms x_i · x_j = x_k for i, j, k ∈ {1, ..., 7} together with 2^(2^(x_j)) = x_k for j, k ∈ {1, ..., 7}. If a subsystem S ⊆ A has at most five equations and only finitely many solutions in (ℕ \ {0, 1})^7, must every such solution (x_1, ..., x_7) satisfy x_1, ..., x_7 ≤ 16?
accepted.context_brief: Hypothesis 1 on bounded finite-solution subsystems of A

evidence.quote: Hypothesis 1. If a system of equations S ⊆ A has at most five equations and at most finitely many solutions in (N \ {0, 1})^7, then each such solution (x1, . . . , x7) satisfies x1, . . . , x7 6 16.

accepted.question_text: Are there infinitely many composite numbers of the form 2^(2^n) + 1?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 1. ([3, p. 159]). Are there infinitely many composite numbers of the form 2^(2^n) + 1?

accepted.question_text: Are there infinitely many prime numbers of the form 2^(2^n) + 1?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 2. ([3, p. 158]). Are there infinitely many prime numbers of the form 2^(2^n) + 1?

accepted.question_text: Let B be the set of all equations x_i · x_j = x_k for i, j, k ∈ {1, ..., 6} together with x_j! = x_k for distinct j, k ∈ {1, ..., 6}. If a subsystem S ⊆ B has only finitely many solutions in positive integers x_1, ..., x_6, must every such solution satisfy x_1, ..., x_6 ≤ (24!)!?
accepted.context_brief: Hypothesis 2 on bounded finite-solution subsystems of B

evidence.quote: Hypothesis 2. If a system of equations S ⊆ B has at most finitely many solutions in positive integers x1, . . . , x6, then each such solution (x1, . . . , x6) satisfies x1, . . . , x6 6 (24!)!.

accepted.question_text: Are the only positive integers x for which x! + 1 is a perfect square the values x = 4, 5, and 7? Equivalently, are the only positive-integer solutions of x! + 1 = y^2 the pairs (4, 5), (5, 11), and (7, 71)?

evidence.quote: It is conjectured that x! + 1 is a square only for x ∈ {4, 5, 7}, see [8, p. 297].

accepted.question_text: Let C be the set of all equations x_i · x_j = x_k for distinct i, j ∈ {1, ..., 6} and k ∈ {1, ..., 6}, together with x_j! = x_k for distinct j, k ∈ {1, ..., 6}. If a subsystem S ⊆ C has only finitely many solutions in positive integers x_1, ..., x_6, must every such solution satisfy x_1, ..., x_6 ≤ 720!?
accepted.context_brief: Hypothesis 3 on bounded finite-solution subsystems of C

evidence.quote: Hypothesis 3. If a system of equations S ⊆ C has at most finitely many solutions in positive integers x1, . . . , x6, then each such solution (x1, . . . , x6) satisfies x1, . . . , x6 6 720!.

accepted.question_text: Determine all positive-integer solutions (x, y) to x(x + 1) = y!. In particular, are the only such solutions (1, 2) and (2, 3)?

evidence.quote: Theorem 3. Hypothesis 3 implies that if the equation x1(x1 + 1) = x2! has at most finitely many solutions in positive integers x1 and x2, then each such solution (x1, x2) belongs to the set {(1, 2), (2, 3)}.
The question of solving the equation x(x + 1) = y! was posed by P. Erdos, see [1].
